word_order: SOV — verbs/predicates consistently appear clause-finally (e.g. '맞는 거 같애', '판단을 한 후에', '돌아온거야'), with objects/complements preceding them.
punctuation_present: sometimes — many utterances end with '.' or '?' but several run-on speech clauses have no terminal punctuation at all
register: spontaneous conversational speech (transcribed dialogue/interview, informal spoken Korean with fillers, self-corrections, and trailing connective endings)
non_boundary_traps: -는데 (often continues into next clause rather than ending it)
그 (demonstrative filler, not a clause boundary)
뭐 (filler particle, not a topic marker boundary)
이런 거/이런데 (vague nominalizers that attach to preceding clause)
target_language_risks: Korean drops subjects/objects freely (pro-drop), so a segment translated alone into English may lack an explicit subject or object recoverable only from prior context
Sentence-final connective endings like -는데/-고/-다가 signal continuation, not completion; cutting there yields incomplete English clauses
Honorific/speech-level endings (-습니다 vs -어/아) affect register and must stay consistent across segments
Topic markers (은/는) and case particles can be omitted in casual speech, making constituent boundaries ambiguous
Repeated hedging fillers (뭐, 그, 이제) have no direct English equivalent and may be mistakenly treated as segment boundaries
notes_for_prompt_writer: This is casual spoken Korean transcript with frequent fillers, self-repairs, and run-on clauses linked by connective endings (-는데, -고, -다가, -면서). Segment primarily at true clause-final endings (-어/아, -습니다, -거든, -잖아) and at strong punctuation (., ?, !), but treat -는데/-고 as weak/continuing boundaries requiring lookahead before splitting. Never start a new segment with trailing punctuation or with a demonstrative/filler like 그/뭐/이제 that grammatically attaches to the prior clause; instead attach these to the following clause only if they begin a new sentence after a period.
